comparison: Both evaluations agree that the EWAS findings (C32-C35) replicating GFI1 associations are well-supported. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with appropriate statistical evidence; peer reviewers acknowledged this as a strength with no concerns raised.

Both evaluations agree that the replication of known GFI1 associations (C44-C47) is well-supported. OpenEval notes this provides validation but is confirmatory rather than novel; peer reviewers accepted these findings without concern.

Major disagreement on MRS construction and validation (C36-C37). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with highly significant p-values; peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, stating 'the authors cannot fully independently validated their MRS' due to insufficient smokers in South Asian cohort and limited array coverage.

Disagreement on MRS associations with smoking status (C38-C40). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED; peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, criticizing that 'the conclusion on generalizability of the maternal smoking risk score is currently not supported by their data' and that 'the inclusion of the START cohort in certain figures is not warranted.'

Partial overlap on MRS predictive performance (C49-C50). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with high AUCs; peer reviewers included these claims in their UNCERTAIN evaluation, expressing concerns about validation limitations and array coverage.

Both address lack of dose-response replication in FAMILY (C48). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, acknowledging the lack of replication may reflect timing/duration differences; peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, suggesting this inconsistency may reflect underpowered analyses.

Disagreement on MRS associations with birth outcomes (C41-C43). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with appropriate statistical evidence; peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, finding it 'interesting' and 'highly novel' but expressing concern that associations 'could be associated with factors other than smoking alone (e.g., pollution).'

Partial overlap on meta-analysis consistency (C53-C54). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED showing consistent effects across populations; peer reviewers included these in UNCERTAIN evaluation, concerned about confounding factors and lack of data on second-hand smoke and pollution.

Both address biological mechanisms (C58). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED though mechanistic link not directly tested; peer reviewers included in UNCERTAIN evaluation, noting the finding warrants further investigation but interpretation is limited by missing confounding data.

Both rate findings in South Asian cohort (C79-C80) as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes mechanism not definitively established; peer reviewers similarly express concern about alternative explanations (pollution, second-hand smoke) and note 'data on this was not available.'

Both agree that MRS associations with postnatal smoking exposure (C51-C52) are SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes this suggests MRS reflects ongoing environmental exposure; peer reviewers accepted these findings without specific concerns as part of MRS validation.

Disagreement on null findings for respiratory outcomes (C105). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting this is a negative result that may reflect limited follow-up or power; peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, stating 'Future exploration should also include a strong focus on more diverse health outcomes.'

Partial overlap on persistence of associations (C55). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED; peer reviewers included in UNCERTAIN evaluation focused on respiratory outcomes, suggesting lack of associations is a limitation rather than definitive.

Major disagreement on generalizability claims (C64). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting multi-ancestry approach represents important contribution; peer reviewers rate as UNSUPPORTED, stating 'their conclusion on generalizability of the maternal smoking risk score is currently not supported by their data.'

Disagreement on conclusions about South Asian populations (C67-C68). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED though notes interpretation requires careful consideration of confounding; peer reviewers rate as UNSUPPORTED due to inability to validate in sufficient numbers of South Asian smokers.

Partial overlap on MRS portability across populations (C104). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with caution about lack of active smokers; peer reviewers included in UNSUPPORTED evaluation, stating 'the overall statement that smoking-associated MRS are portable across populations are not fully supported.'

Both agree that cohort smoking characteristics (C26-C27) are SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes these describe important cohort characteristics; peer reviewers accepted these observations but identified low smoking rates as a major limitation affecting statistical power.

Both agree on smoking prevalence data (C88-C89). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED; peer reviewers also accepted these observations as SUPPORTED but explicitly noted 'Numbers of mothers who self-reported any smoking was very low likely resulting in underpowered analyses.'

Disagreement on targeted array performance (C69-C71). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting comparable performance though 'equally powerful' may be overstated; peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, viewing limited coverage as compromising comprehensiveness and noting array 'was designed in 2016' with 'omission of potentially relevant sites.'

Partial overlap on study design (C30). OpenEval rates methodological approaches as SUPPORTED; peer reviewers included targeted array use in UNCERTAIN evaluation, identifying it as a significant weakness due to limited CpG coverage.

Both rate speculative interpretations of South Asian findings (C56-C57) as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes explanations not directly tested; peer reviewers similarly note finding is interesting but 'data on this [second-hand smoke and/or pollution] was not available,' limiting ability to test alternative explanations.
